subChunks.title: CompletableFuture Basics
subChunks.hookHtml: Raw Future.get() blocks your thread like a stone wall. CompletableFuture lets you chain transformations, attach callbacks, and compose async pipelines — all without blocking a single thread.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Creating a CompletableFuture

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync() runs a Supplier on the common ForkJoin pool (or a provided executor) and returns a CompletableFuture<T> you can chain. CompletableFuture.runAsync() does the same for Runnable (returns CompletableFuture<Void>).

CompletableFuture<String> cf = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
    // runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
    return "Arcane";
});

Transforming Results: thenApply, thenAccept, thenRun

These methods attach callbacks that execute when the future completes. They form a pipeline — each receives the previous stage's result.

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Arcane")
    .thenApply(s -> s + " Surge")          // transforms: String -> String
    .thenApply(String::toUpperCase)          // transforms: "ARCANE SURGE"
    .thenAccept(s -> System.out.println("Result: " + s)) // consumes, returns Void
    .thenRun(() -> System.out.println("Pipeline complete")); // no input, no output

join() vs get()

Both block the calling thread until the result is available. The difference: get() throws checked exceptions (InterruptedException, ExecutionException), forcing you to handle them. join() wraps exceptions in unchecked CompletionException — cleaner in lambda chains.

String result = cf.join(); // unchecked — cleaner in pipelines
// vs
String result2 = cf.get(); // throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException

Error Handling: exceptionally & whenComplete

exceptionally() catches any exception in the pipeline and returns a fallback value — like a catch block for async code. whenComplete() runs a callback with either the result OR the exception (similar to finally).

CompletableFuture<String> safe = CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> { throw new RuntimeException("Spell fizzled!"); })
    .exceptionally(ex -> "Default Spell"); // fallback value on error

safe.thenAccept(System.out::println); // prints "Default Spell"
safe.join();

completeExceptionally & Manual Completion

You can manually complete a CompletableFuture with complete(value) or fail it with completeExceptionally(throwable). This is useful when bridging callback-based APIs into the CompletableFuture world.

CompletableFuture<String> manual = new CompletableFuture<>();
// somewhere later, after async work finishes:
manual.complete("Result ready");
// or on failure:
manual.completeExceptionally(new RuntimeException("Failed"));

storyBeats.text: The Academy's ancient scrying orbs could only show one vision at a time — each mage had to wait, blocking the chamber, until the orb went dark before the next could look. A new invention changed everything.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: CompletableFuture is the modern crystal ball. Instead of staring into it until an answer appears — blocking all else — you attach instructions for what to do when the vision arrives, then walk away.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: thenApply transforms the result — like an alchemist changing lead to gold. thenAccept consumes it — like delivering the gold to the vault. thenRun fires afterward with no regard for the result.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And when a spell goes wrong, exceptionally() catches the disaster and returns a safe fallback. Never let an unhandled exception shatter your pipeline.

storyBeats.speaker: Error Handling
storyBeats.text:
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { throw new RuntimeException(); })
    .exceptionally(ex -> "Default Spell")
    .thenAccept(System.out::println)
    .join(); // prints "Default Spell"
With CompletableFuture, the scrying chamber handles dozens of visions simultaneously — no mage standing idle, each vision feeding the next step of the arcane pipeline automatically.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a CompletableFuture pipeline: use supplyAsync to supply the string "Arcane". Chain thenApply to append " Surge". Chain another thenApply to convert to uppercase. Chain thenAccept to print "Final spell: " + the result. Chain thenRun to print "Pipeline complete". Call .join() at the end of the chain to block until done.

Also demonstrate exceptionally: create a separate future that throws a RuntimeException, use .exceptionally(e -> "Spell fizzled"), join it, and print the result.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between thenApply, thenAccept, and thenRun. When would you use exceptionally() versus whenComplete()? And explain why join() is often preferred over get() inside lambda chains.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory, build a CompletableFuture pipeline: supplyAsync("Arcane"), append " Surge", uppercase, print "Final spell: ARCANE SURGE", then print "Pipeline complete". Also create a second future that throws an exception, handle it with exceptionally to return "Spell fizzled", and print that result.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The default thread pool used by supplyAsync() and runAsync() when no executor is provided. Shared JVM-wide; fine for CPU tasks but avoid for blocking I/O (use a dedicated pool instead).
The interface CompletableFuture implements, defining the chainable methods (thenApply, thenAccept, etc.). Allows swapping implementations without changing pipeline code.
Like thenApply() but executes the transformation on a separate thread from the pool, rather than on the thread that completed the previous stage.
A two-argument callback receiving both the result and the exception (one will be null). Unlike exceptionally(), handle() runs regardless of success or failure and can transform both cases.
The unchecked exception join() throws (wrapping the original cause) when the CompletableFuture completed exceptionally. Access the real cause via getCause().
The challenge of slowing a producer when consumers can't keep up. CompletableFuture has no built-in backpressure — for that, explore reactive libraries like Project Reactor or RxJava.
A modern approach (previewed in Java 21+) where async tasks have a clear scope and lifetime tied to a parent task. Aims to make concurrent code safer and easier to reason about than raw futures.
Java 21 feature (Project Loom) — lightweight threads managed by the JVM. Blocking virtual threads is cheap, reducing the need for async pipelines for I/O-bound work.

questions.questionHtml: Which CompletableFuture method consumes the result (returns CompletableFuture<Void>) without transforming it?
questions.explanationHtml: thenAccept(Consumer) receives the result and performs a side effect, returning CompletableFuture<Void>. thenApply(Function) transforms the result. thenRun(Runnable) ignores the result entirely.
Start with 10, multiply by 3 → 30, add 5 → 35. The thenAccept prints "Value: 35".

questions.questionHtml: This code should print a fallback when an exception occurs, but it throws instead. What is wrong?
questions.correctAnswer: exceptionally() is missing — add .exceptionally(ex -> "Fallback") before join()
questions.explanationHtml: join() rethrows the exception as a CompletionException if the future completed exceptionally. Add .exceptionally(ex -> "Fallback") before join() to catch the error and return a default value.

questions.questionHtml: When should you provide a custom Executor to supplyAsync(supplier, executor) instead of using the default common pool?
options: When the task is CPU-bound and fast
When the task performs blocking I/O such as database or network calls
When you want the task to run on the main thread
questions.correctAnswer: When the task performs blocking I/O such as database or network calls
questions.explanationHtml: The common ForkJoinPool is sized for CPU-bound work. Blocking I/O tasks submitted there can starve other async tasks. Use a dedicated ExecutorService for I/O-bound work so blocking threads don't clog the shared pool.

subChunks.title: Combining & Composing Futures
subChunks.hookHtml: One arcane calculation at a time is never enough. Real spells combine multiple async results — weaving damage rolls, defence checks, and element lookups into a single decisive outcome.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
thenCompose — Chaining Dependent Futures

thenCompose() is the flatMap of CompletableFuture. Use it when the next step itself returns a CompletableFuture — otherwise you'd get CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>> with thenApply.

CompletableFuture<String> spellName = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Fire");
CompletableFuture<String> fullSpell = spellName.thenCompose(name ->
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> name + "ball") // another async step
);
System.out.println(fullSpell.join()); // "Fireball"

thenCombine — Zipping Two Independent Futures

thenCombine(other, BiFunction) waits for both futures to complete independently, then combines their results. The two futures run in parallel.

CompletableFuture<Integer> damage  = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 70);
CompletableFuture<Integer> defense = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 30);

CompletableFuture<Integer> netDamage = damage.thenCombine(defense,
    (dmg, def) -> dmg - def
);
System.out.println("Net damage: " + netDamage.join()); // "Net damage: 40"

allOf — Wait for Everything

CompletableFuture.allOf(cf1, cf2, ...) returns a CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when ALL supplied futures complete. Useful for fan-out then collect patterns.

CompletableFuture<String> f1 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "A");
CompletableFuture<String> f2 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "B");
CompletableFuture<String> f3 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "C");

CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2, f3).join(); // wait for all
System.out.println(f1.join() + f2.join() + f3.join()); // "ABC" (order guaranteed now)

anyOf — First to Complete Wins

CompletableFuture.anyOf(cf1, cf2, ...) returns a CompletableFuture<Object> that completes as soon as the first of the supplied futures completes. Useful for racing redundant requests.

CompletableFuture<Object> fastest = CompletableFuture.anyOf(
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Slow spell"),
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Fast spell")
);
System.out.println(fastest.join()); // whichever finishes first

whenComplete — Cleanup Callback

whenComplete(BiConsumer<T, Throwable>) runs a callback with either the result or exception (one is null), without transforming the value. It's always executed, like a finally block, making it ideal for logging or releasing resources.

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Spell cast")
    .whenComplete((result, ex) -> {
        if (ex != null) System.out.println("Failed: " + ex.getMessage());
        else System.out.println("Success: " + result);
    })
    .join();

storyBeats.text: The Grand Duel required three simultaneous calculations — damage roll, defense roll, and elemental affinity — each drawn from a different arcane register. No single oracle could provide all three.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: thenCombine is your spell for zipping two independent futures. Both oracles consult simultaneously, and when both reply, you merge their answers into a single truth.

storyBeats.speaker: thenCombine
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: allOf waits for every oracle to report. anyOf names the winner of a race. Choose wisely — waiting for all is thorough; racing to the first is fast but unpredictable.

storyBeats.speaker: allOf Pattern
storyBeats.text:
CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2, f3).join();
System.out.println("All spells resolved");

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: thenCompose is flatMap — use it when your next step itself returns a future. Without it, you'd have a future inside a future, like a scroll sealed inside another scroll.
The Grand Duel resolved cleanly: damage and defense calculated in parallel, combined in milliseconds, the net damage printed to the scoreboard before the dust settled.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Part 1: Create futureA = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 70) (damage) and futureB = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 30) (defense). Use thenCombine to compute damage - defense and print "Net damage: " + the result. Call join().

Part 2: Create 3 separate futures using supplyAsync. Use CompletableFuture.allOf() to wait for all three. After allOf().join(), print "All spells resolved".
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between thenApply and thenCompose with a concrete example. When would combining two futures with thenCombine be better than running them sequentially? What does allOf return and why can't you get the individual results from it directly?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory, create two CompletableFutures: one supplying 70 (damage) and one supplying 30 (defense). Combine them with thenCombine to compute damage minus defense, then print "Net damage: " + result. Also create 3 futures and use allOf to wait for all, then print "All spells resolved".

rabbitHoleTerms.description: thenApply wraps the returned value in a new future (use for synchronous transforms). thenCompose flattens a returned future — use when your callback itself returns a CompletableFuture, avoiding nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>.
allOf() returns CompletableFuture<Void> — you can't get results from it directly. Pattern: after allOf.join(), call join() on each individual future (they're all done at that point).
anyOf() returns the result of the first completing future but does not cancel the others — they continue running. Use carefully if tasks have side effects.
Like thenCombine but runs the BiFunction on a thread from the pool instead of the completing thread. Prefer when the combining logic is heavy.
Java 21 introduced virtual threads that make blocking I/O cheap. Much async code written with CompletableFuture could be simplified to straightforward blocking code on virtual threads.
A specification (implemented by Project Reactor, RxJava) for async stream processing with backpressure. CompletableFuture handles single-value async; reactive handles streams of values.
Non-async thenApply/thenAccept run on the thread that completed the previous stage. Async variants (thenApplyAsync) run on the pool. Mixing these can cause subtle ordering issues.
Java 9+ method on CompletableFuture that completes the future exceptionally with TimeoutException after a given duration — cleaner than manually scheduling cancellation.

options: CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when all futures complete
void — it blocks until all futures complete
questions.correctAnswer: CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when all futures complete
questions.explanationHtml: allOf() returns CompletableFuture<Void>. It doesn't aggregate results. After calling allOf(...).join(), you retrieve individual results by calling join() on each original future.
futureA completes with 100, futureB with 25. thenCombine subtracts: 100 - 25 = 75. Prints "Result: 75".

questions.questionHtml: This code tries to chain two async operations but ends up with a nested future. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
questions.correctAnswer: Replace thenApply with thenCompose to flatten the nested future
questions.explanationHtml: When the mapper in thenApply itself returns a CompletableFuture, you get CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>. Use thenCompose instead — it flattens the result to CompletableFuture<T>.

questions.questionHtml: You need to call two independent services and combine their results. Which approach is most efficient?
options: Call service A with supplyAsync, join(), then call service B with supplyAsync, join(), then combine
Use thenCombine with two supplyAsync calls so both run in parallel
Use thenCompose to chain service A then service B sequentially
Create a single supplyAsync that calls both services sequentially
questions.correctAnswer: Use thenCombine with two supplyAsync calls so both run in parallel
questions.explanationHtml: thenCombine with two independent supplyAsync calls runs both in parallel, halving the total wait time compared to sequential calls. Calling join() between calls forces sequential execution, losing the parallelism benefit.
